title: Volume 6 · Production Costing, Scrap and Subcontracting
subtitle: Lessons 5–8: what a finished unit really cost, how scrap changes the answer, and where subcontracting sits in the ledger
outcomes: Read a production cost and reconcile it to the BOM
Handle scrap so the good units carry the loss
Subcontract an operation and keep material control
Explain variance between planned and actual cost to a production manager

slides.title: Read the finished cost before you defend it
bullets: Finished cost is materials consumed plus operations recorded, divided by good units
The stock ledger row is the proof, not the report total
A cost that differs from the BOM has exactly three usual causes
Cost reviewed weekly stops being an argument at month end

rows: One line in the production worksheet

slides.notes: The arithmetic here is deliberately identical to the BOM, because the first production run should show no variance. Once a client sees that the system agrees with the recipe, they trust it when the numbers later diverge. Introduce variance only after the clean case is understood, or the learner will assume every difference is a system error.

slides.title: Cost per unit, proved three ways
bullets: Materials, operations and total must agree from the entry, the stock ledger and the BOM
Valuation per unit appears in the stock ledger row and the stock balance report
A rounding difference of a cent is normal, a difference of ten per cent is not
Any difference must be explained in the worksheet before the period closes
slides.notes: Three ways of seeing the same number is the fastest way to build confidence in a new system. Ask the learner to read the figure off the entry, off the ledger and off the balance sheet item, then to explain why all three agree. When they can do that unprompted, they can survive any costing meeting.

slides.title: Scrap one unit and let the good units carry it
bullets: Scrap is a quantity decision, not a cost adjustment typed into a journal
The total production cost stays the same while the good quantity falls
Cost per good unit therefore rises, and the finished stock carries that higher value
Scrap needs a reason code, because the causes are process, material or machine

rows: Stock Entry type Material Issue from Main, quantity 1
Scrap - assembly defect, cost centre Assembly

slides.notes: Two thousand three hundred across nine units is two hundred fifty five point five six, and that is the number the owner needs to see, because the loss is now visible in the value of the remaining stock. If the scrap were journalled away, the nine good units would look cheaper than they are and the next quotation would be priced on a lie.

slides.title: Subcontract an operation and keep control of the material
bullets: Subcontracting sends material out and buys a service back, and both must be recorded
The subcontractor warehouse is where your material sits while someone else holds it
The purchase receipt of the service adds that cost to the finished valuation
Sending material without a transfer is how stock disappears in a subcontracting business

rows: SM-ASM with operation Powder Coating marked subcontract
Service item Powder Coating, 10 units at 12.00

slides.notes: Twelve ringgit of coating on a two hundred thirty assembly gives two hundred forty two, and the subcontractor warehouse must end at zero. That zero is the control: if material is still sitting with the subcontractor after the service receipt, someone is holding your stock without a document, which is a finding worth raising the same day.

slides.title: What scrap does to the remaining value
bullets: Total production cost is unchanged by scrap, and the good units carry it
The stock value stays at 2,300.00 with nine units, so the report shows the loss
A scrap account only appears if you configured the entry to expense it directly
Recalculate the selling price implication before the next quotation goes out

rows: 1 unit issued with a reason and cost centre

slides.notes: Two hundred fifty five fifty six against a three hundred fifty selling price leaves ninety four forty four, roughly twenty seven per cent, down from thirty four. That fall is the real cost of the defect, and it belongs in the next pricing conversation rather than the scrap bin. Show the learner the margin before and after, and the quality discussion starts by itself.

slides.title: Proof the service and the material both landed
bullets: Material out, service in, material back: three movements and one valuation
The service cost is only in stock if the receipt was against the subcontracting order
The subcontractor warehouse must return to zero, or material is unaccounted for
Subcontract purchase invoices still carry tax, and it is input tax like any purchase
slides.notes: The two numbers that matter are zero and two hundred forty two: nothing left with the supplier, and every returned unit carrying the service cost. If either is wrong, the receipt was raised against the wrong order or the transfer never happened, and both are visible in the same screen. Checking this weekly prevents the year-end scramble that subcontracting projects always produce.

slides.title: Cost components and where they land
bullets: Every ringgit of production cost must land in inventory, not in an expense account
Capacity cost is labour and machine time, and it needs a rate the client can defend
Scrap and rework are cost of quality, and they belong in the same work order
Subcontracting adds an external service cost, which is still inventory until sale

rows: Work in progress, then finished goods
Cost of the remaining good units

slides.notes: This is the table to leave with a manufacturing client, because their accountant will ask where each element sits and their production manager will ask who controls it. Answering both columns in one page is what turns a system implementation into a costing conversation the client trusts.

lab.title: Lab · Cost a build, scrap a unit and subcontract an operation
steps: Read the completed manufacture entry and confirm 2,300.00 total cost
Prove 230.00 per unit from the entry, the stock ledger and the stock balance
Issue one assembly as scrap with a reason and a cost centre
Confirm nine units now carry the full 2,300.00 and recompute the unit cost
Create a subcontracting operation on the BOM for powder coating at 12.00
Raise the purchase order and transfer ten assemblies to the subcontractor warehouse
Receive the service and confirm the new valuation of 242.00 per unit
Prove the subcontractor warehouse balance is zero after receipt
lab.done: Done when scrap leaves nine units at 255.56 each, the subcontracted units carry 242.00, and no material remains in the subcontractor warehouse.

quiz.question: A build costs 2,300.00 and one of ten units is scrapped. Cost per good unit becomes what?
quiz.why: Total cost stays at 2,300.00 while the good quantity falls to nine, so each unit carries 255.56.

quiz.question: How should scrap be recorded?
options: A stock entry with a reason code
quiz.why: Scrap is a quantity event, so it needs a stock entry with a reason, which also keeps the cost with the good units.

quiz.question: In subcontracting, where does your material sit while the supplier works on it?
quiz.why: ERPNext holds subcontracted material in a subcontractor warehouse so the balance proves what is with the supplier.

quiz.question: What should the subcontractor warehouse balance be after the service is received?
quiz.why: All transferred material should return, so a non-zero balance means material is unaccounted for and needs immediate investigation.

quiz.question: Which production cost lands in finished goods valuation?
quiz.why: Production cost includes material, operations and bought-in services used in the build, all of which stay in inventory until sale.

memory.spine: Total production cost is fixed; the only question is how many good units must carry it, and scrap never answers that with a journal.

device.label: Good units carry the bad ones
expansion: Finished cost is materials consumed plus operations recorded, divided by good units
Scrap is a quantity decision on the document, never a cost typed into a journal
Total production cost is unchanged by scrap, so the good units absorb it
Subcontracting is material out, service in and material back: three movements, one valuation
Every ringgit of production cost lands in inventory, not in an expense account

cards.q: How is cost per finished unit calculated?
cards.a: Materials plus operations, divided by good units, with scrap in the numerator and never quietly subtracted.

cards.q: One of ten units is scrapped. What happens to total cost?
cards.a: It stays the same and the nine good units carry it, so unit cost rises.
As a quantity on the manufacture entry or a separate scrap entry, not as a journal.

cards.q: How many movements does subcontracting create?
cards.a: Three: material out to the subcontractor, the service received, and the finished material back.
In inventory value. An expense account here means the stock was under costed.

trap.what: Scrap is written off to an expense account at the end of the month instead of on the document.
trap.why: Finished units then carry a cost that excludes the loss, the true unit cost is understated, and the expense appears where nobody looks.

narration: Once a client has built something, the next question is what it cost, and the answer has to survive an argument. A completed build of ten assemblies carries two thousand of material and three hundred of labour, so two hundred thirty each, and the entry, the stock ledger and the stock balance must all say the same thing. Scrap is where costing gets real: one unit fails, the total cost does not move, and the nine good units now carry two hundred fifty five fifty six each. Subcontracting adds a bought-in service, twelve ringgit of coating, and a warehouse that must return to zero. Materials, labour, scrap, service: four components, one valuation, and a worksheet that lets the production manager and the accountant argue with numbers instead of opinions. Teach the four components in order, and insist on the worksheet, because a costing conversation without evidence becomes a personality contest, and the consultant is always the outsider in that room.
